---
title: "Which fin section for an IOM?"
subtitle: "2D CFD of symmetric NACA sections at model-yacht Reynolds numbers, ranked by race time"
author: Kliment Mamykin
date: 2026-10-16
date-modified: 2026-10-17
date-format: "D MMMM YYYY"
license: "CC BY"
language:
  title-block-published: "First published"
  title-block-modified: "Updated"
abstract: |
  The fin of an International One Metre (IOM) radio-controlled yacht makes the side force that lets it
  sail upwind. It works at Reynolds numbers of 3×10⁴ to 2×10⁵, where laminar separation bubbles set
  much of the drag. This project compares symmetric NACA sections 6–12\ % thick at chords of 80–100 mm
  with 2D simulations that model laminar–turbulent transition (OpenFOAM, k-ω SST with the
  Langtry–Menter transition model). Sections are ranked not by their drag coefficient but by the race
  time they cost: drag and leeway at equal side force upwind, and drag at zero angle downwind.
  Time-accurate simulations showed that at 4° every section sheds vortices, and that the steady
  solver had overestimated lift there by 4–16\ %. That changed the ranking. Different winds favour
  different fins: NACA 0007 at 100 mm chord is best in light and medium air, and NACA 0008 at 100 mm
  is best at 1.5 m/s, by about 1\ % of race time (a result still being checked). For one fin in all
  winds, NACA 0007 at 100 mm is the best all-round choice on current evidence: on average it gives
  away about 0.3\ % of race time, roughly 1.4 boat lengths per race, against changing fins for each
  wind.
---

## Previous state of the art {#sec-prior}

::: {.callout-note}
## Partly drafted
The fins-in-use and stiffness parts summarise two research notes,
[iom-fins-on-the-market.md](https://github.com/kmamykin/iom_cfd/blob/main/docs/research/iom-fins-on-the-market.md)
and [fin-stiffness.md](https://github.com/kmamykin/iom_cfd/blob/main/docs/research/fin-stiffness.md).
The aerofoil and transition parts are still short. Numbers on this page come from this project unless a
source is cited; product figures are the makers' own claims.
:::

**Fins in use.** The class rules leave the fin almost free [@iom-rules-2026]:

* any material no denser than lead, so carbon is legal in the fin (though not in the hull);
* no minimum thickness, and at most 20 mm thick above the bottom 60 mm;
* a keel of 2.2–2.5 kg and a draft of 370–420 mm.

Every fin on the market with stated dimensions is a tapered carbon blade, about 80–100 mm in chord at
the hull and 63–75 mm at the bulb, 350–360 mm below the hull, 6–7\ % thick (about 5–6 mm).

* SAILSetc sells a 7\ % fin, 90 → 75 mm [@sailsetc-370iom].
* Craig Smith sells a 6\ % fin, 90 → 75 mm [@cs-cf1].
* Rob Nelson sells a fin of 100 → 70 mm, thickness not stated [@rn-gp].

No maker names its section. Graham Bantock's fins have used custom low-Reynolds-number sections by
David Hollom since 1992 [@hollom2008]. The designs winning world championships (V12, VISS, Venti, K2)
come with their own fins, whose dimensions aren't published [@iomica-hof]. Designers agree that thin
is fast: "the thinnest is best, around 6\ %", with a longer chord if the fin needs strength
(Bantock, as recalled in a forum). Proposals for a minimum fin thickness were defeated in the 1990s
[@bantock-iom1]. The typical leeway in the No. 1 rig is about 3° [@gilbert-finforce]. *Not found:*
any published comparison of fin sections or chords for IOMs in terms of race time.

**Low-Reynolds-number aerofoils.** Wind-tunnel polars at Re ≈ 10⁵ [@selig1989] show how laminar
separation bubbles set the drag of thin sections. This project validates against those polars
(@sec-validation).

**Predicting transition.** RANS turbulence models can be combined with a transition model
[@menter1994; @langtry2009]. Their known weak spot is separation bubbles.

**Surface finish and trips.** Roughness on model yachts is covered by @klaka2022, and
boundary-layer trips on low-Reynolds-number aerofoils by @lyon1997. The project's research note
[surface-roughness.md](https://github.com/kmamykin/iom_cfd/blob/main/docs/research/surface-roughness.md)
has the details.

**Fin stiffness.** It matters mainly for holding the bulb, by limiting sag at high heel and
oscillation in waves. Its value in race time hasn't been measured (@sec-conclusion).

**What this project adds:**

* a ranking by race time rather than drag coefficient, with leeway and the downwind leg counted;
* a check of the steady solutions against time-accurate ones;
* the ranking at three boat speeds.

## Methodology {#sec-method}

### Simulating a fin section

Each simulation is a 2D slice of the fin: one section at one angle of attack and one boat speed, in
fresh water at 15 °C. It uses OpenFOAM v2512 [@openfoam] with the k-ω SST turbulence model
[@menter1994] and the γ-Re~θ~ transition model of Langtry and Menter [@langtry2009]. The transition
model predicts where the boundary layer stays laminar, separates, reattaches or turns turbulent,
which at these Reynolds numbers decides most of the drag. It needs the turbulence of the incoming
water, Tu. Nobody has measured Tu on a model-yacht pond, so it is a parameter (0.1\ % and 1\ %), not a
constant.

Two solvers are used:

* **Steady** (simpleFoam) finds a flow that doesn't change in time. It is cheap enough to sweep
  hundreds of cases per run, but where the real flow is unsteady its answer can be wrong
  (@sec-transient).
* **Time-accurate** (pimpleFoam) follows the flow in time, here for 30 chord flow-throughs (the time
  the water takes to pass the chord 30 times). The forces are averaged over the last 6. It costs
  8–13 hours per case on one core.

The mesh (@fig-mesh) is a structured C-grid written directly by the project's own generator: 90,112
hexahedral cells, wall-normal grid lines, the first cell sized for y⁺ ≈ 0.5 so that the viscous
sublayer is resolved, and a far field 50 chords away. Doubling the cell count changes drag by 0.1–0.2\ %
at 4° and 0.8–1.7\ % at 6°, and lift by under 0.4\ % (study `mesh-finalists`).

![The medium C-grid for NACA 0007 at 100 mm chord: the whole domain (every 4th grid line), the
section, and the leading edge. Drawn by the same code that writes the simulation
mesh.](_generated/mesh.png){#fig-mesh}

### Validation {#sec-validation}

NACA 0009 at Re = 10⁵ against wind-tunnel data from Princeton [@selig1989]:

![NACA 0009 at Re 10⁵, coarse mesh, Tu 0.1\ %, steady solver. The transition model (used for every
result on this page) gets lift within 6\ % up to 8°; drag is 10\ % high at 4° and 25\ % high at 8°, where
a laminar separation bubble dominates. The fully turbulent model has too much drag at low angles
because it misses the laminar flow.](_generated/validation.svg){#fig-validation}

At upwind angles of 2–5° the transition model is good enough to *rank* sections. Absolute drag is
uncertain by roughly 10–25\ %. Likely causes, roughly in order: the transition model's handling of
separation bubbles; the tunnel's effective turbulence; steady solutions of an unsteady flow at 4°; mesh
resolution; and scatter in the experiment itself.

### From a section to a fin

Each simulation gives a lift and drag coefficient, C~l~ and C~d~. They are scaled to the whole fin,
with span b = 0.36 m below the hull, chord c and dynamic pressure q = ½ρV²:

$$
\begin{aligned}
F &= C_l\, q\, c\, b \\
D &= C_d\, q\, c\, b + \frac{F^2}{2\pi\, q\, e\, b^2}
\end{aligned}
$$

The second term of D is the induced drag of a lifting line, with the hull as a reflection plane and
span efficiency e = 0.9. All fins have the same span, so at equal side force their induced drag is the
same: it adds to the total but doesn't reorder the fins.

### Compare at equal side force

The sails decide how much side force the fin must make, not the fin. So every fin is compared at the
same three forces, the **loads**: what one reference section (0009/80) makes at 2°, 4° and 6°. At
1 m/s these are 1.15 N (light), 6.69 N (working) and 8.33 N (high). For each fin, interpolating along
its lift curve gives the angle it needs, and along its drag curve its drag, at that force
(@fig-equal-force).

![The two steps of the comparison at 1 m/s, Tu 0.1\ %, for the four best fins. Left: the angle each
fin needs to make the load. Right: its drag at that load. Diamonds are the time-accurate 4° points
that replaced the steady ones (dashed); the steady points overestimated lift, so every fin needs more
angle than the steady curves suggested.](_generated/equal-force.svg){#fig-equal-force}

A longer chord makes the same force at a lower angle. The difference in angle is the difference in
**leeway**, because the 3D part of the angle depends on span and force, not chord.

### Race time

Two costs upwind, and one downwind (@fig-course):

![Left: upwind, the boat heads 39° off the true wind [@gilbert-vmg] and slides 3° sideways, so it tracks
at 42° [@gilbert-finforce]. Right: the fin's angle of attack α is the leeway; its side force balances the sails and its
drag slows the boat. Downwind the fin makes no side force and sits at α = 0.](_generated/course.svg){#fig-course}

* **Drag slows the boat.** Extra drag ΔD costs a fraction of the leg's time of
  $$\text{drag loss} = \frac{\Delta D}{V\,\mathrm{d}R/\mathrm{d}V},$$
  where dR/dV is the slope of the boat's total resistance with speed. V dR/dV ≈ 1.35 N at 1 m/s,
  estimated from hull, fin, bulb and rudder friction. At that slope 0.01 N of extra drag costs 0.74\ %
  of the leg.
* **Leeway lengthens the path.** Sailing D metres to windward takes D / cos θ metres of track, with
  θ = 42°. One more degree of leeway costs tan θ · Δα ≈ **1.57\ %** of the leg.
* **Downwind** the fin's drag at 0° counts, at the same boat speed.

With equal time upwind and downwind, a fin's loss is half the sum of the three, measured against the
best fin and averaged over the three loads. The resistance slope is the least certain input, so every
result is also computed with it doubled; tables show both as "×1 / ×2".

An example at working load: 0008/90 is 0.92\ % behind 0007/100. Its extra upwind drag (0.016 N) costs
0.60\ %, its extra 0.36° of leeway 0.29\ %, and its extra downwind drag 0.03\ %. The full method is in
[methodology.md](https://github.com/kmamykin/iom_cfd/blob/main/projects/foil2d/methodology.md).

### Robustness

A fin can win on average and still lose badly somewhere. So the ranking is repeated for each boat speed
(0.75, 1 and 1.5 m/s) and each combination of water turbulence (Tu 0.1\ % and 1\ %), resistance slope
(×1 and ×2) and solver (steady or time-accurate points). A fin's **regret** in each case is how far it
is behind the best fin there; the largest regret says how badly the choice could turn out.

Boat speed stands in for the wind: light air at about 0.75 m/s, medium at 1 m/s, fresh at 1.5 m/s.
That mapping is an assumption; the boat's actual speeds depend on the rig and the conditions.

## Process and studies {#sec-studies}

The work went in small steps, each a study with a question. Its answer set up the next one
(@tbl-studies).

::: {#tbl-studies}
| when | study | question | answer |
|:----|:----------------|:----------------|:------------------------|
| 11\ Oct | validation | Does the transition model match wind-tunnel data at Re 10⁵? | Well enough to rank sections (@sec-validation). |
| 12\ Oct | selection run 1: 0006, 0009, 0012 × 80, 100 mm; 360 cases | How do thickness and chord trade off? | A thin, short fin wins at light load and a longer chord at high load. At working load the optimum lies between 6\ % and 9\ % thick. |
| 13\ Oct | selection run 2: 0006–0012 × 80, 90, 100 mm; 450 cases | Where between 6\ % and 9\ %? | Thin sections lose at working load because their laminar boundary layer separates at the leading edge. NACA 0012 is out. |
| 13\ Oct | mesh check | Is the mesh fine enough to separate the finalists? | Yes: medium is within 0.2\ % of fine at 4°. |
| 13\ Oct | selection run 3: four finalists at Tu 0.1\ %; 100 cases | Does calmer water change the order? | Calmer water means *more* drag at 4–8°: the laminar bubble grows. |
| 13\ Oct | analysis: leeway and both legs | What does the drag difference cost on the race course? | Counting leeway favours longer chords again; 0008/90 looked like the safest all-rounder. |
| 13\ Oct | selection run 4: 0007/90, 0007/100, 0008/100; 75 cases | Are the thinner, longer sections better still? | Possibly, but the steady 4° solutions oscillated too much to tell. |
| 14\ Oct | time-accurate check 1: 10 cases | Are the oscillating steady points right? | At 6° yes for the 0009 sections, within 0.5\ %. At 4° every section sheds vortices, and 15 flow-throughs were too few to settle. |
| 15\ Oct | time-accurate check 2: 8 cases continued to 30 flow-throughs | Where do the 4° forces settle? | Lift 4–16\ % below steady. 0007/100 moves to first, 0008/90 to fourth. |
| 17\ Oct | time-accurate check 3: the top four at 2° and 6°, and at 0.75 and 1.5 m/s; 15 of 16 cases | Does that hold at other angles and speeds? | At 0.75 and 1 m/s, yes. At 1.5 m/s 0007/100 switches to a leading-edge bubble and drops to last of the four. The steady 6° drag of the 0007 and 0008 sections was 4–6\ % high. |
| running | time-accurate check 4: 2 cases | Is that 1.5 m/s result real? | Pending. |

The studies so far. Each has a dated findings log in the repository.
:::

### Steady and time-accurate {#sec-transient}

The steady solver's 4° solutions for the most promising thin sections never settled: their drag
oscillated by up to 22\ %. Time-accurate runs showed why: the flow itself is unsteady. A laminar boundary layer runs to
about a third of the chord, separates, and rolls up into vortices that travel over the rear half.

Getting a reliable time average took two lessons (@fig-force-history):

* **An impulsive start leaves a slow lift build-up.** Lift approaches its final value as the Wagner
  function predicts [@wagner1925; @jones1938]: about 95\ % after 15 flow-throughs, 99\ % after 30. The
  first runs stopped at 15 and were still drifting. They were continued to 30 from where they stopped.
* **Starting from the steady solution settles in about 10 flow-throughs.** The mean is the same either
  way.

![Lift at 4° and 1 m/s. Left: 0007/100 started from rest, continued at 15 flow-throughs; the
dash-dot line is the Wagner build-up scaled to the final mean. Right: 0009/100 started from the steady
solution. Thin lines are the instantaneous lift, which oscillates by about 10\ % as vortices are shed;
the forces are averaged over flow-throughs 24–30 (shaded).](_generated/force-history.svg){#fig-force-history}

The settled means are checked by comparing the two halves of the averaging window: they agree to
within 1.3\ %. Halving the time step changes lift and drag by about 1\ %.

## Visualisations of the findings {#sec-findings}

### What the flow does at 4°

::: {#fig-shedding}
{{< video assets/shedding-video.mp4 >}}

Flow speed and streamlines around NACA 0009 at 4° and Re 10⁵ (time-accurate, coarse mesh; 12
snapshots, about one and a half shedding cycles). The laminar boundary layer on the suction side
separates and rolls up into vortices that travel over the rear half and into the wake.
:::

### How the flow changes with angle

::: {#fig-angle-sweep}
{{< video assets/flow-angle-sweep.mp4 >}}

NACA 0009 at 80 mm, 1 m/s, Tu 1\ %, steady solutions at 0°, 2°, 4°, 6° and 8°, one frame per angle (the
colours are explained below). As the angle rises, separation moves forward: near the trailing edge at
0–2°; a bubble at mid-chord that reattaches at 4° (from 28\ % to 69\ % of the chord); a short bubble at
the leading edge with turbulent flow behind it at 6–8°. Drag rises from C~d~ 0.014 to 0.040.
:::

### A gallery of flows {#sec-gallery}

Each picture is the suction side of one simulation, coloured by the flow speed along the surface:

* **pale:** the free stream;
* **amber:** faster than the free stream;
* **dark:** the slow layer next to the wall (the boundary layer);
* **blue:** flow going backwards.

Pictures from time-accurate runs show a single instant. Captions give the section and chord, the
angle, the boat speed, the water turbulence (Tu) and the solver.

**Healthy: attached flow.**

### What the steady solver got wrong

![Lift and drag coefficients at 4° and 1 m/s, steady against time-accurate. Every section makes about
the same time-accurate lift, C~l~ 0.39–0.40; the steady solver spread them from 0.41 to 0.47, and the
thick sections were the most wrong.](_generated/steady-vs-transient.svg){#fig-steady-vs-transient}

At 6° the flow is steady, but the steady drag was still 4–6\ % high for the 0007 and 0008 sections
(within 0.5\ % for 0009). At 4° the steady points were too optimistic about lift and too pessimistic
about drag, at 0.75, 1 and 1.5 m/s, and not by the same amount for every section. That reordered the
fins. At 2° the 0008 sections, which looked perfectly steady in the steady solver, shed strongly.

Race-time loss of the four best fins by boat speed, % behind the best of the four: estimated

"Worst" is the largest loss at any of the three speeds.
:::

**Different winds favour different fins.** NACA 0007 at 100 mm is best at 0.75 and 1 m/s, by about
0.5\ % of race time (2 boat lengths). At 1.5 m/s it is last of the four, 1\ % (about 4 boat lengths)
behind NACA 0008 at 100 mm. The reason is a change in the flow (@fig-leading-edge-bubble): at 0.75
and 1 m/s its boundary layer separates near mid-chord and sheds vortices, like every other section; at
1.5 m/s it separates right at the leading edge, reattaches turbulent and stays attached, with twice
the skin friction. The same thing made the thinnest section, NACA 0006, lose at working load in
selection run 2. This rests on one simulation, and a check is running.

![NACA 0007 at 100 mm, 4°: pressure and skin friction on the suction side at 0.75 and 1.5 m/s (the
final instant of time-accurate runs). Negative skin friction is reversed flow.](_generated/leading-edge-bubble.svg){#fig-leading-edge-bubble}

## Conclusion {#sec-conclusion}

**Different winds favour different fins.**

* **Light and medium air (0.75–1 m/s boat speed): NACA 0007 at 100 mm.** It is about 0.5\ % of race time
  (2 boat lengths per race) ahead of the next best, NACA 0007 at 90 mm, and 0.7–0.8\ % (3 boat lengths)
  ahead of NACA 0008 at 100 mm.
* **Fresh air (1.5 m/s): NACA 0008 at 100 mm.** It is about 1\ % (4 boat lengths) ahead of
  0007/100, whose flow switches to a high-drag leading-edge bubble at that speed
  (@fig-leading-edge-bubble). This rests on one simulation; the check is running.

Few sailors change fins with the wind, so the question is what one fin for every wind gives away
(@tbl-fin-choice).

::: {#tbl-fin-choice}
{{< include _generated/fin-choice.md >}}

What each fin gives away against the best fin for each wind (the one you'd fit if you could change
fins), % of race time: estimated resistance slope / doubled. "Average" weights the three winds
equally; boat lengths per race at about 4 per 1\ % (an estimate).
:::

**Best all-round: NACA 0007 at 100 mm**, on current evidence.

* It gives away the least on average: 0.33\ % of race time, about 1.4 boat lengths per race. NACA 0007
  at 90 mm gives away 0.42\ % and NACA 0008 at 100 mm 0.49\ %.
* All of its cost is in fresh air. If the running check confirms the leading-edge bubble, and finds it
  already at 1.25 m/s, it loses over a wider range of winds, and NACA 0008 at 100 mm would likely become
  the better all-round fin (an estimate).
* NACA 0007 at 90 mm is the most even (never more than 0.55\ % behind), but it is the least stiff of
  the three.

**Stiffness.** At IOM speeds the bulb loads the fin more than the water does: at 30° heel the part of
a 2.4 kg bulb's weight across the fin is about 12\ N, against about 7\ N of side force. A soft fin lets
the bulb sag to leeward at high heel, which costs righting moment, and lets fin and bulb oscillate in
waves. One designer describes a boat (a Ten Rater, a larger radio class) that "would slow and spurt
unpredictably in waves" until a stiffer fin was fitted [@gilbert-finpos]. Nobody has published how much stiffness is worth in race time, and the
leading designers put thinness first, getting stiffness from the chord and the layup. A fin's bending
stiffness scales roughly with chord × thickness³, so at 100 mm NACA 0007 is about 50\ % stiffer at the
root than a 7\ % fin with a 90 mm chord, and NACA 0008 at 100 mm is another 30–50\ % stiffer (estimates
for the same construction). Stiffness doesn't rule out 0007/100; if the boat sails a lot in waves at
high heel, or the bulb sits well aft of the fin, 0008/100 is the safer side. The details and the
sources are in the research note
[fin-stiffness.md](https://github.com/kmamykin/iom_cfd/blob/main/docs/research/fin-stiffness.md).

**How much is at stake.** The right fin for the wind is worth up to about 1\ % of race time (4 boat
lengths); between the three best all-round choices, about 0.2\ % on average (under a boat length). By
comparison, sanding finer than 400–600 grit gains less than half a boat length, but a dirty, slimy or
unfair hull can cost as much as a poor section choice or more [@klaka2022]. Choose the section, *and*
keep the boat clean and fair.

**Why the order is not certain:**

* The fresh-air result for 0007/100 rests on one simulation (being checked).
* At 0.75 and 1.5 m/s only the 4° points are time-accurate; 0.5 m/s has none.
* The simulations are 2D, with a constant chord. Tip, bulb, hull junction, heel and taper are not
  modelled.
* The resistance slope and the water turbulence are estimates, the hull and rudder are assumed to make no
  side force, and every wind is weighted equally.
* The shedding has not been validated against measurements at these Reynolds numbers.

**Against what is sold.** The recommended thickness, 7\ %, is what the market sells and what designers
recommend. The chord is not: the simulations favour 90–100 mm, because a longer chord needs less leeway,
while commercial fins taper from 80–100 mm at the hull to 63–75 mm at the bulb (a mean of about
75–85 mm). The 2D model can't weigh taper, which moves lift and bending moment towards the root and
saves weight at the tip. In practice, "NACA 0007 at 100 mm" means a 7\ % fin at the long end of what is
sold; a 3D comparison of a tapered fin is the open question.

**What would change it:**

* the running check of 0007/100 at 1.25 and 1.5 m/s;
* a hull resistance curve, to replace the estimate;
* a 3D check of 0007/100 against 0008/100, and of a tapered 7\ % fin (for example 100 → 70 mm) against
  a constant 100 mm chord;
* a bench test of a real fin's stiffness: the tip drop with the keel held horizontal and the bulb on.

## Reproducing this {.appendix .unnumbered}

Everything is in [the repository](https://github.com/kmamykin/iom_cfd): the simulation setup
(`projects/foil2d/`), every study file, and a findings log per study with the numbers behind each
conclusion. Simulations run in Docker (`uv run iomcfd run foil2d/<study>`) or on Google Cloud Batch.
This page is built from `site/` with Quarto; its charts are drawn from the small data files below,
which `iomcfd site export` copies out of the runs. The code is under the
[MIT licence](https://github.com/kmamykin/iom_cfd/blob/main/LICENSE); the text, figures and data on
this page are under CC BY 4.0. Reference data from other sources keeps its own terms.
